sections.html:
A deed to Massachusetts land is recorded at the registry of deeds for the county or registry district where the land lies. That rule comes from G.L. c. 183, section 4. Without recording in that registry, a conveyance of a fee simple estate cannot be enforced against most outside parties.

Three groups are bound regardless: the grantor, the grantor's heirs and devisees, and anyone who actually knew about the deed. Even so, a signed deed should never sit in a drawer. A later buyer, a creditor or an attachment could beat an unrecorded deed in a priority dispute.

Sellers rarely file the deed themselves. After the money changes hands, the closer carries it to the correct registry. That is usually the attorney working for the buyer or the buyer's lender. It still pays to know where it is headed and how to confirm it arrived.

Massachusetts runs two title systems side by side. Between eighty and ninety percent of Commonwealth properties are recorded land.

Recorded land is the familiar kind. Every document gets a book and page number and can be viewed online. Registered land works differently: a Land Court decree called a Certificate of Title lists the owner, describes the parcel and notes any encumbrances.

Registered land is still handled at the county registry, because the Land Court's registered land districts are housed inside the county registries. It does change what you file. Norfolk County, for example, publishes two columns on its fee schedule, one for recorded land and one for the Land Court side, and a document needing both needs two separate checks.

  • Recorded land: indexed by book and page, searchable online.
  • Registered land: backed by a Land Court Certificate of Title.
  • Unsure which you own: ask the registry or your closing attorney.

sections.h2: What a deed must contain to be accepted
sections.html:
G.L. c. 183, section 6 requires the grantee's full name, residence and post office address on any deed offered for recording, along with a recital of the full consideration.

The consideration is the entire price, with nothing subtracted for liens or encumbrances the buyer assumes or that stay on the property. A deed not given for a set sum of money must describe whatever was given instead. These recitals are recorded along with the deed.

Here is the part that surprises sellers. A missing item does not make the deed invalid, but a register of deeds is barred from accepting it. The deed can be perfectly good between the parties and still bounce at the counter.

  • The buyer's full legal name and mailing address, on the deed or endorsed on it.
  • The price in dollars, figured before any mortgage the buyer takes over is subtracted.

Recording involves two separate items: a registry recording fee and the deeds excise tax. Each registry sets and posts its own fees, so the safest figure is the one on your registry's current schedule.

As one example, the Norfolk County Registry of Deeds fee schedule lists a deed at $156.00 for recorded land and $155.00 on the Land Court side. A mortgage is $206.00, a mortgage discharge is $106.00 per marginal reference, a declaration of homestead is $36.00 and a municipal lien certificate is $81.00. A one dollar postage and return charge applies to documents mailed or recorded in person. Electronic filings skip it as of July 1, 2025.

Another county may charge differently, so get the exact figure from that registry or your attorney.

sections.h2: How the deeds excise tax works
sections.html:
This tax is figured on the price stated in the deed, per $500 or fraction of $500. G.L. c. 64D, section 1 sets the base at $2.00 for each additional $500 or fractional part, and $1.50 in Barnstable County.

It reaches deeds with consideration above one hundred dollars, not counting liens or encumbrances that remain. Exempt are instruments given to secure a debt and deeds where the Commonwealth, a city or town, or the United States or their agencies is a party.

Norfolk County collects $2.28 for each $500 and any fraction, and its worked example puts the tax on a $155,000 deed at $706.80. Pay what your own registry's current schedule says. Norfolk wants an attorney's check or bank check for the tax, apart from the recording fee, and charges nothing when consideration is under $100.

  • The stated price drives the amount, so the consideration on the deed matters.
  • The purchase agreement says who pays, so check with your attorney before signing.
  • Any part of a $500 block counts as a whole block, which means the figure rounds up.

Send the original signed deed, the recording fee and the excise tax payment, plus anything else your registry requests.

Lenders and title insurers usually insist on an attorney, so the closing attorney typically handles all of this. In Massachusetts, attorneys are part of real estate sales by law and by custom. The Supreme Judicial Court's decision in Real Estate Bar Association v. National Real Estate Information Services, 459 Mass. 512 (2011), held that a lender's closing requires an attorney's substantive participation.

  • The signed, acknowledged original deed, not a photocopy.
  • The recording fee, by check or electronic payment as the registry directs.
  • The excise tax on its own bank or attorney's check.

Norfolk accepts cash or check for recording and copy fees. A document recorded on both the Land Court and registry sides needs its own check for each.

sections.h2: Checking that your deed was recorded
sections.html:
Look the document up on masslandrecords.com or your registry's own site. You can also sign up for an alert service. Masslandrecords.com is where to find copies of your deed and mortgage too.

The Secretary of the Commonwealth offers a consumer notification service that emails you whenever a new document is recorded against your property. Norfolk County's registry also has a page about deed scams.

The assessors' office is another source. Owners can pull up their deed online next to the property record card used to produce the tax bill. If a recorded deed does not appear after a few days, call the registry and ask your closing attorney to follow up.

sections.h2: Other state rules that touch a sale
sections.html:
Two state rules matter beyond recording. G.L. c. 93, section 70 has the mortgagee's attorney certify title to both the mortgagor and the mortgagee when a purchase money first mortgage is granted on an owner-occupied dwelling for up to four families.

The home inspection waiver regulation, 760 CMR 74, bars sellers of certain residential properties from making an offer depend on a waived inspection, or from taking offers from buyers who plan to waive one. Whether it reaches your sale turns on the property and the buyer, so ask your attorney.

Liens, back taxes and a muddled chain of title tend to surface at recording. Bring them up with your attorney early.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Massachusetts?
faqs.a: At the registry of deeds serving the county or district where the property sits. Recording there is what makes the deed good against most third parties under G.L. c. 183, section 4.

faqs.q: How much is the excise tax when I sell my house?
faqs.a: The tax is a set amount per $500 of the price stated in the deed. The Norfolk County registry collects $2.28 per $500 and shows $706.80 on a $155,000 deed, while G.L. c. 64D, section 1 gives a base of $2 per $500. Check your registry for the current rate.

faqs.q: Can a deed be valid but not accepted for recording?
faqs.a: Yes. A missing grantee address or consideration recital does not affect validity under G.L. c. 183, section 6, but a register of deeds may not accept a deed that lacks them.

faqs.q: Does every Massachusetts property use the same title system?
faqs.a: No. Most properties, an estimated eighty to ninety percent, are recorded land, and the rest are registered land with a Certificate of Title through the Land Court.

faqs.q: How do I get a copy of my recorded deed?
faqs.a: Search masslandrecords.com or ask your registry. Norfolk County lists copies at $1.00 per page, plus a postage charge for copies ordered by mail.
